title: Trustworthy Agentic AI: A Comprehensive Cybersecurity and Systems Survey on Threat Landscapes, Defense Architectures, and Open Challenges

    Title:Trustworthy Agentic AI: A Comprehensive Cybersecurity and Systems Survey on Threat Landscapes, Defense Architectures, and Open Challenges
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:The transition from passive foundation models to autonomous, goal-directed agentic AI systems has introduced unprecedented capabilities by coupling recursive cognitive reasoning loops, persistent memory architectures, live tool execution planes, and multi-agent collaboration topologies. However, granting probabilistic neural cores execution authority across filesystems, networks, and cloud infrastructure dissolves classical security perimeters: natural language simultaneously serves as input data, internal control code, and communication protocols, exposing a Turing-complete blast radius where untrusted data represents executable instructions. This survey delivers a comprehensive systems-security reference framework for trustworthy agentic AI, synthesizing 206 foundational studies and regulatory standards. We formalize the general agent architecture as a stateful 5-tuple and establish a 6-dimensional trustworthiness taxonomy covering security, safety, privacy, explainability, fairness, and accountability. We systematically analyze threat surfaces across intra-execution loops and interaction planes, formulate a multi-layered zero-trust defense-in-depth architecture integrating Dual-LLM isolation, Capability-Based Access Control, kernel eBPF probes, and sandboxed runtimes, review standardized evaluation benchmarks, and map technical controls to international AI governance frameworks.

report.summary: A new survey synthesizes 206 studies to map security threats in autonomous agentic AI and propose a zero-trust, defense-in-depth architecture spanning sandboxing, capability control, and governance.
report.background: Foundation models are rapidly being wrapped in autonomous agents that plan, remember, call tools, and collaborate with other agents. That shift hands probabilistic neural networks real execution authority over filesystems, networks, and cloud infrastructure, dissolving the security perimeters that classical cybersecurity assumed. Traditional defenses were built for deterministic code and human operators, not for systems where a document, a webpage, or another agent's message can be interpreted as an instruction. Early incidents — prompt injection, credential exfiltration, runaway tool loops, supply-chain poisoning of agent plugins — exposed the gap, while regulators (the EU AI Act, NIST's AI Risk Management Framework) demanded technical controls that did not yet have a consolidated reference. This survey responds by mapping the threat landscape, formalizing agent architecture, and translating governance principles into concrete systems-security mechanisms.
key_points: The paper formalizes a general agent as a stateful 5-tuple, capturing recursive reasoning loops, persistent memory, live tool execution, and multi-agent topology, and builds a 6-dimensional trustworthiness taxonomy: security, safety, privacy, explainability, fairness, and accountability.

The core vulnerability is linguistic: natural language serves simultaneously as input data, internal control code, and inter-agent protocol. Untrusted content therefore becomes executable instruction, creating what the authors call a Turing-complete blast radius across any resource the agent can touch.

Threat surfaces are systematically mapped across two layers — intra-execution loops (memory poisoning, reasoning hijacking, tool abuse) and interaction planes (agent-to-agent, agent-to-tool, agent-to-human), where trust boundaries are ambiguous and often implicit.

The proposed defense is multi-layered zero-trust: Dual-LLM isolation separating privileged planning from untrusted content parsing, Capability-Based Access Control for least-privilege tool grants, kernel eBPF probes for runtime monitoring, and sandboxed execution runtimes.

The survey also reviews standardized evaluation benchmarks and maps each technical control to international AI governance frameworks, giving compliance and engineering teams a shared vocabulary rather than two disconnected checklists.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this reframes agent security as a systems-engineering discipline rather than a prompt-engineering afterthought: vendors shipping autonomous products will increasingly be expected to demonstrate isolated planners, scoped capability tokens, and auditable runtime telemetry before enterprise adoption. For developers, the practical takeaways are least-privilege tool permissions, sandboxed execution, dual-LLM separation of untrusted content, and instrumentation via eBPF or equivalent observability — skills that suggest an emerging 'agent security engineer' role. For regular users, the paper implies that the agents holding your credentials, inbox, and file access should come with consent prompts, provable scope limits, and post-hoc audit trails. Governance frameworks gain a technical counterpart, making compliance verifiable rather than declarative.
report.tools: Follow the paper's own stack first: Dual-LLM isolation, Capability-Based Access Control, kernel eBPF probes, and sandboxed runtimes. For sandboxing, watch gVisor, Firecracker, WebAssembly/Wasmtime, and Docker with seccomp profiles; for runtime monitoring, Falco, Tetragon, and Cilium; for guardrails, NVIDIA NeMo Guardrails and Guardrails AI. Threat taxonomies worth bookmarking include OWASP's LLM and Agentic AI Top 10, MITRE ATLAS, and NIST's AI RMF. For empirical testing, AgentDojo and InjecAgent offer agent-specific red-team benchmarks.
